newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch mid-sized firms continue on takeover trail.
newsitem.headline: Dutch mid-sized firms continue on takeover trail.

text.p: Dutch companies will continue to seek growth outside the Netherlands through takeovers in the years ahead, corporate representatives told an investors symposium on medium-sized bourse-listed firms on Tuesday.

Cable maker NKF and tank storage and shipping group Van Ommeren said they are planning acquisitions in the next few years. Earlier today, Heidemij said it would buy fellow engineering consultancy DHV.
Van Ommeren's financial manager Roelof Hendriks said his company expected to announce a takeover in the shipping sector within the next six months but he declined to identify the firm.

After several years of rising profits and cost-cutting, many Dutch firms now have ample liquid assets. Given low interest rates, they increasingly use these for takeovers rather than reap the interest gains, financial analysts said.
These healthy corporate war chests have produced a wave of foreign takeovers by Dutch companies in the last few weeks.
These included acquisitions by Akzo, Dutch PTT, Pakhoed, Wolters Kluwer, Aalberts, Hoek Loos and SHV.
Van Ommeren has been filling in gaps in its world-wide network of tank storage and shipping activities and will continue to do so, in Asia and South America in particular.
Hendriks said Van Ommeren expects to finance its plans from its cash flow and existing assets.
"We will try to stay within our cash flow," he said, adding that given Van Ommeren's strong balance sheet it need not issue shares to finance takeovers before the year 2000.
"We have got a lot of leverage left," Hendriks said. Takeovers would only be considered if they immediately contributed to earnings per share, he said.

Cable maker NKF's financial director Robert de Bakker told the symposium, which was organised by merchant bank Insinger de Beaufort, NKF would seek growth in the market for complex cable projects which offers large contracts and higher added value.
"We want a larger role in that market as we have the knowledge to do more than just make cables," he said. Currently, this sector generates about five percent of NKF's turnover.

But also in the power and telecommunications cables markets, which now form the bulk of NKF's activities, the company seeks organic and takeover growth in the higher added value segments with a strong focus on growing earnings per share.
Last year, NKF boosted its size by taking over the cable division of former majority shareholder Nokia.

Earlier, Heidemij said it planned to buy Dutch civil engineering consultancy DHV. Heidemij board member Jan van den Ochtend said his firm was also about to enter the Asian and Latin American markets. In five to 10 years, Heidemij wants to generate about 20 percent of its gross revenue from these areas.
A short-term goal is to raise the company's profit margin to five percent of sales from the current 3.5 percent through cost cuts, better project management and fixed price arrangements.
